questions.prompt: What is a secure SDLC?
options: A tool that scans a finished program for viruses
Security built into every phase of making software
Security added at the very end, just before launch
A law about who owns the code a crew writes

questions.prompt: In which SDLC phase do you decide what security properties the software must have?
In which SDLC phase do you model threats before any code is written?
Patching software after release belongs to which phase?
Actively trying to break the software before release belongs to which phase?
Why is a flaw caught in design cheaper to fix?
options: It is still just a decision on paper
Design flaws never need to be fixed at all
Code cannot have any security flaws
Designers are paid less than coders

questions.prompt: A flaw is found after release. What can that cost?
options: A small change to the requirements document
Nothing, flaws after release are always harmless
Rewriting code, telling users, fixing damage
Only a quick note added to the next version

questions.prompt: What is threat modeling?
options: Hiring an outside crew to watch the logs at night
Writing the code first and testing it later on
Making a 3D model of the server room for planning
Asking how it could be attacked, before coding

questions.prompt: In STRIDE, what does the S stand for?

Making a system unavailable is which STRIDE category?
A normal user gains admin access. Which STRIDE category is this?

Why go through each STRIDE category instead of asking "is this secure?"
options: It forces a specific answer for each kind of misuse
STRIDE only has one category to think about
It replaces the need to test the software at all
It is quicker than asking just one general question

questions.prompt: What is the OWASP Top 10?
options: A list of the most common web app weaknesses
A list of the ten best firewalls on the market
A list of the ten strongest passwords to use
A list of the ten largest data breaches ever

questions.prompt: A user reaches data their role should never allow. Which OWASP issue is this?
What is a hardcoded credential?
options: A password that unlocks only one account
A password stored only in one person's memory
A password that is changed every single hour

Anyone who reads the file has the password

It stops users from logging in at all

options: Remove it and change that password
Leave it, the app works fine
Rename the config file to hide it away
Add a second password next to it

The user controls everything on their device
Servers always trust the client by design

options: Enforcing every one of the important rules

questions.prompt: Which client practice is risky?
options: A check repeated on the server

options: Remote tools never work over very long distances
Admins cannot type commands from far away

options: It uses up too much of the network's bandwidth
Legacy ports cannot be monitored by anyone
Commands and passwords travel in the clear
Closing it makes the admin password stronger

questions.prompt: Why must admin accounts meet the strong-password standard too?
options: Admin accounts are never targeted by attackers
The standard only applies to admin accounts
Admins can choose any password they like
